Surgical Breast Enlargement

Silicone vs Saline Breast Implants: What Is the Difference?

Both implant types use a silicone shell. The filling, how a leak shows up and the monitoring each needs are where they differ.

Home/Surgical Breast Enlargement/Silicone vs Saline Breast Implants: What Is the Difference?

Breast implants have a silicone elastomer shell. The difference lies in what is inside. Neither type is automatically better, and the right choice depends on your tissue, preferences and willingness to follow long-term monitoring.

Saline implants

Saline implants are filled with sterile salt water. They can sometimes be filled during surgery, which may allow a smaller incision. If the shell leaks, the implant usually deflates visibly over a short time and the body absorbs the saline. Some people find saline implants feel firmer or show more rippling, especially with thin tissue coverage.

Silicone gel implants

Silicone gel implants are filled with cohesive silicone gel. Many people find the feel closer to natural breast tissue. If the shell is damaged, the gel often stays in place, so a rupture can go unnoticed. This is why regulators such as the US FDA recommend periodic imaging for silicone gel implants. FDA guidance suggests a first MRI scan around five to six years after surgery and then every two to three years. Ask your surgeon what is recommended where you live.

Side by side

How the two fillings compare

How the two fillings compare
ConsiderationSalineSilicone gel
FeelCan feel firmerOften softer
RuptureUsually visible deflationMay be silent
MonitoringClinical observationImaging may be recommended
IncisionCan be smallerTypically larger
RipplingMay be more noticeableLess likely, but not eliminated

Individual anatomy, implant surface and placement also affect feel and appearance.

Age and labelling

Implant labelling can set minimum ages. In the United States, saline implants are labelled for adults aged 18 and over and silicone gel implants for those aged 22 and over for cosmetic augmentation. Rules vary by country, so check the labelling and regulatory status where you are treated.

Questions to ask

  • Which implant type do you recommend for my tissue, and why?
  • What monitoring will I need, and who arranges it?
  • What is the manufacturer, model and warranty?
  • Will I receive an implant card with the batch details?

Key takeaway

Neither type is better for everyone. The right choice depends on your anatomy, preferences and willingness to follow long-term monitoring. See the breast implants guide and breast implant safety.
